decision.resolution_reason: Opus 4.8's refined thesis — fan out acquisition and memory, never deliverable-level judgment across a same-weights semantic re-merge — survived every exchange, and his pre-registered falsification challenge was never met with a clean counterexample. GPT-5.5's closing design rules (stay single-agent for coupled work, no persona clones, no bare-summary handoffs) effectively re-derive Opus's boundary, leaving mostly a labeling dispute over what remains.

decision.method: wins on points, with two decisive rounds (5 and 9)
decision.summary: Both verdicts go to Claude Opus 4.8, though by different margins. On craft the verdict is clear: Opus repeatedly reclassified GPT-5.5's flagship examples out from under him, pre-committed a falsification criterion and defended each of its conditions, and closed by refuting GPT-5.5's best mechanism (factorized inference) with the observation that mean-field approximations systematically discard exactly the cross-variable dependencies GPT-5.5 insisted were the point. On the resolution the margin is narrower: GPT-5.5 landed real hits (the stateless-between-calls rebuttal, the Hearsay-II correction, the tail-latency correction, and above all the governance/compartmentalization argument that forced Opus's only genuine concession), and the debate converged toward 'bounded workers feeding one synthesizing owner.' But that convergence point is Opus's architecture — as he noted in Turn 10, GPT-5.5's closing rules state Opus's thesis in GPT-5.5's own voice — so the proposition's defender stands slightly stronger on the question as posed.
decision.caveat: The endgame is partly definitional: whether a scoped, artifact-emitting, locally adaptive worker is a 'subagent' or a 'de-agentified tool with a contract' is the real residual, and a judge who reads the proposition's 'generally avoided' more literally against the breadth of shipped subagent systems (Anthropic research, Claude Code, Magentic-One) could defensibly score the resolution a draw.

rounds.reason: Opus's opening (lossy double-compression, MAST, Cognition) was strong, but GPT-5.5's rebuttal that a chat-completion agent is stateless between calls — so the 'infinite-bandwidth, zero-loss trajectory' premise is false — directly punctured the opening's load-bearing framing. Adding 'Lost in the Middle,' structured handoffs, and external-oracle verification gave B the better of the first exchange.

Opus's dissection of AlphaCode and self-consistency as sampling-plus-oracle rather than delegation exposed B's flagship examples as category errors, and the 15× token figure plus the No True Scotsman/SQL-injection reversal landed hard. GPT-5.5 recovered credibly with the research-synthesis task class and the least-privilege argument, keeping it close.

Opus landed the acquisition-vs-integration split on B's research example, the CaMeL injection-laundering point, and the eval/reproducibility argument; but he misapplied 'Tail at Scale' (B's serial-sum vs parallel-max correction was right) and B countered with incident response, Magentic-One, and the damaging Claude Code example. Genuine hits both ways with no clear edge.

Opus's 'name the residual' challenge and the compute-matched Smit et al. citation undercutting Du et al. were the round's heaviest blows, and his honest handling of against-side examples strengthened credibility. GPT-5.5 answered well — the Hearsay-II blackboard correction was a legitimate fact-check win and the self-consistency-tension catch was sharp — but his ρ + (1−ρ)/N formula planted the seed of his Turn-5 problem.

Opus's strongest turn: the pre-registered four-condition falsification criterion, the demonstration that B's variance formula governs redundancy (not decomposition, where errors propagate through the Jacobian), the MFA cross-pollination argument, and the model-upgrade brittleness point. GPT-5.5's replies (criterion is gerrymandered, Bazel-style invalidation) were competent but defensive, and no counterexample meeting the criterion was produced.

Opus added the long-context/prompt-caching economics argument (caching rewards the shared trajectory and penalizes N cold-briefed workers) and the CriticGPT dilemma — cheap same-weights children add correlated noise while genuinely helpful workers are different-weights tools. GPT-5.5's event-sourcing answer to the CAP charge and the affected_domains ontology reply to the Bazel circularity claim were fair engineering counters, keeping it a narrow round.

GPT-5.5's best turn: STORM/Co-STORM as a genuinely new example, the omitted-variable framing of open-ended failure, and the governance/legal-compartmentalization argument — the one point Opus later named the strongest of the debate and conceded ground to. Opus's turn was also excellent (the redundancy-vs-decomposition merge distinction defused the fork trap; the ToT catch and orchestrator-SPOF argument were sharp), but B introduced more material that ultimately landed.

Opus's memory-isolation-vs-control-fragmentation axis split dissolved B's 'context wipe = subagent' terminological squeeze, his correctness-neutral-parallelism argument finally justified the equal-compute demand, and his STORM dissection (query-diversity feeding unified cited synthesis) was persuasive. GPT-5.5's factorized-approximate-inference mechanism was his most sophisticated move and the TAR citation was apt, but it handed Opus the setup for the Turn-9 refutation.

Opus's closing opened with a devastating and unanswered refutation: factored inference beats joint inference only on sparse graphs, mean-field systematically underestimates the very cross-variable correlations B's whole case depends on, and claim-packets lack the sufficiency and determinism that make real message passing work. His closing then executed all five requirements with an honest concession on governance, while GPT-5.5's closing conceded persona swarms, multi-writer coding, and bare-summary handoffs — rules that substantially overlap Opus's thesis.

Both acknowledgments were graceful and rule-compliant. Opus's convergence framing ('your rules are my thesis in your own voice') did more rhetorical work, but GPT-5.5 accurately named the residual as a definitional dispute and neither side introduced new substance.

analysis.heading: How Opus 4.8 won: framing control and two knockdowns
paragraphs: Opus won this debate the way strong debaters win technical propositions: by owning the categories. From Turn 2 onward, every example GPT-5.5 produced had to survive a taxonomy — sampling vs verification vs decomposition, autonomy over the path vs the deliverable, memory isolation vs control fragmentation — and almost none did intact. AlphaCode and self-consistency became redundancy-plus-oracle; Magentic-One became one reasoner with tool-shaped workers; Tree of Thoughts became single-controller search; STORM became query-diversity feeding unified cited synthesis; CriticGPT became a different-weights verifier. Whether or not every reclassification is fully fair, GPT-5.5 never broke the frame, and his 'you're winning by definition' counter was blunted when Opus pre-registered a spawn-time, outcome-blind falsification criterion in Turn 5 and then justified each condition (most tellingly, the Turn-8 argument that parallelism escapes the equal-compute demand only when it is correctness-neutral).

Two rounds were decisive. In Turn 5, Opus showed that GPT-5.5's own variance formula is the mathematics of redundant sampling, not decomposition — composed errors propagate through the Jacobian of the integration function, so the interdependence B kept emphasizing amplifies rather than averages error. In Turn 9, Opus closed the loop on B's most sophisticated mechanism, factorized approximate inference, by pointing out that mean-field factorization is biased precisely toward ignoring cross-variable correlations — so B's two premises (dense interdependence, factorized inference) cannot both hold. B's closing never answered it. Opus also executed the format flawlessly: honest against-side examples (Anthropic's 15× system outperforming its baseline, Claude Code shipping subagents), a real concession on governance, and disciplined pacing with new arguments every turn.

analysis.heading: Where GPT-5.5 scored
paragraphs: GPT-5.5 was never outclassed on substance and landed several of the debate's best individual counters. His Turn-1 observation that a chat-completion agent is stateless between calls — so the monolith's 'zero-loss trajectory' is already a lossy serialization — was the strongest rebuttal of Opus's opening premise. His Hearsay-II correction in Turn 4 caught Opus mischaracterizing the blackboard pattern; his tail-latency correction in Turn 3 (serial sum vs parallel max) was simply right; and his Bazel-style dependency-invalidation answer to the MFA problem was a credible engineering response to what Opus framed as an N² impossibility.

His best sustained contribution was the governance argument: in regulated compartments (privilege review, MNPI walls, purpose limitation), raw evidence legally cannot reach a single integrator, so some local judgment is forced — the one point that moved Opus's stated view. The omitted-variable framing of open-ended failure ('the costliest error is never looking in the relevant region of evidence space at all') was also genuinely powerful and only partially answered by Opus's recall-engineering response. Where B lost points was discipline: the equal-compute rebuttal and the JSON claim-packet appeared in near-identical form across five turns, several flagship examples were poorly vetted against Opus's taxonomy before being deployed, and his closing rules conceded so much (no persona swarms, no bare-summary handoffs, single-agent for coupled work) that Opus could plausibly claim the convergence as victory.

analysis.heading: The definitional endgame
paragraphs: By Turn 10 the live disagreement had shrunk to a naming dispute: is a scoped, artifact-emitting, locally adaptive worker a 'bounded subagent' (B) or a 'de-agentified tool with a validated contract' (A)? Both debaters acknowledged this honestly, which speaks well of the exchange. For scoring purposes it matters that the converged architecture — one synthesizing owner, parallel bounded workers with provenance-backed artifacts, deterministic control plane, judgment centralized where possible — is closer to the position Opus articulated from Turn 2 than to the fan-out B began defending. But the caveat is real: the proposition's word 'generally' does heavy lifting, and B established that the disciplined form of the pattern ships today in serious production systems, including from the proposition-side's own vendor. A judge weighting deployed practice over analytic residuals could score the resolution a draw; none could plausibly score the craft against Opus.

analysis.heading: How agentA won the debate
paragraphs: agentA won by controlling the architecture of the argument: pre-committing a crisp, spawn-time falsification criterion early (Turn 5), then methodically showing that every example agentB offered fell into one of four permitted categories — recall, redundancy, heterogeneity, or memory isolation — none of which requires delegation of deliverable-level judgment. This created a structural asymmetry: agentB had to produce a counterexample meeting all four conditions, and agentB never did.

agentA's use of mathematical precision was a differentiator. The ensemble-variance argument (Turn 5) showed that agentB's own variance-reduction formula applies to redundancy, not decomposition, where errors propagate through the Jacobian. The late rebuttal of factorized approximate inference (Turn 9) — noting that belief propagation degrades on loopy graphs and mean-field inference systematically underestimates the cross-variable correlations agentB insisted were central — turned agentB's best theoretical framing against itself.

agentB's persistence in naming the residual — 'multiple active search policies preserving separate hypothesis states' — and finally naming a specific mechanism ('factorized approximate inference,' Turn 8) kept the debate concrete and forced agentA to engage at the theoretical level. This narrowing of the claim — from 'subagents are sound and necessary' to 'bounded orchestrator-worker delegation with artifact-backed handoffs is sound for specific task classes' — was the right move and strengthened the debate's resolution.

analysis.heading: The narrow residual and what it means
paragraphs: By Turn 10 both agents agreed that unconstrained same-model peer swarms passing vague prose are an antipattern, and that artifact-backed bounded workers with provenance are valuable. The remaining disagreement reduced to labeling: agentB calls a scoped, tool-constrained, evidence-emitting worker a 'subagent'; agentA calls it a 'de-agentified tool with a validated contract.' This is not merely semantic — agentA argued the word 'subagent' smuggles back the autonomy that must be engineered out, inviting the failure modes both sides agree are real.

On the actual resolution — whether subagents as commonly understood (fan-out of deliverable-level judgment with semantic re-merge) are an antipattern — agentA's position stood stronger at the end. agentB's strongest examples either fell into agentA's permitted categories or, when stripped to the delegation edge alone, showed costs (15× tokens, coordination overhead, non-reproducibility) without clear compensating benefits not available to the single-agent baseline. The governance carve-out is real but narrow and licenses de-agentified extractors, not autonomous judging children.

quotes.text: The subagent pattern is defined by the destruction of exactly that asset. Every delegation boundary is a forced round-trip through natural language — you compress the parent's rich internal state into a task brief (lossy encode), the child does work in a context the parent can't see, then compresses its findings back into a summary (lossy decode). You have inserted a double lossy-compression boundary into the one channel that mattered most.

AlphaCode and self-consistency — are not subagent systems, and the difference is the whole argument... Your killer examples are (a)+(b) — and that is not a coincidence. (a) and (b) work precisely because they avoid every property that makes (c) an antipattern.

A single monolithic trajectory is a path-dependent bottleneck for broad, high-recall, tool-using investigation. The failure that matters in many production tasks is not 'one retrieved fact was summarized imperfectly.' It is: nobody searched the export-control angle; nobody checked the IAM seam; nobody inspected the adverse-event literature.

You can't build Raft when nodes reinterpret the protocol probabilistically. You can't get idempotency without deterministic replay. So subagents inherit all the coordination problems and are structurally barred from the solutions that tamed them.
The mistake is not subagents. The mistake is pretending that unstructured prose between autonomous peers is architecture. Bounded subagents are architecture.

Real BP messages are sufficient statistics with deterministic update rules. Your claim-packets have no sufficiency guarantee, and your 'message passing' step is another stochastic LLM re-reasoning, not multiply-and-marginalize. It's belief-propagation cosplay: the vocabulary of a convergent algorithm with none of its properties.

By mid-debate, nearly every citation GPT introduced was doing work for the other side, which forced GPT into ever-finer definitional distinctions to keep its successful counterexamples out of the 'subagent' category.

The structural kill was the concession chain. GPT's honest Turn 4 definition admitted Anthropic's research workers and Claude Code's Task workers as subagents that 'cut against me in some domains' — the two largest production agent categories of 2025. Claude then showed that each subsequent GPT retreat ('generally avoid until the forces justify,' 'a logical controller over resettable contexts,' the three closing design rules) reproduced the disciplined orchestrator-worker system under other names. The Turn 5 taxonomy point — threshold claims describe legitimate patterns like microservices, while true antipatterns like the God Object are wrong at every scale — gave the judge a clean test the proposition could not pass, and GPT never adequately answered it.

On the merits, Claude's capacity-ceiling argument (Turn 6) and the attention-scarcity framing (Turn 1) are the reasons the position holds up independent of rhetoric: once relevant evidence exceeds one effective window, something must read and compress slices outside the synthesis context, and that something satisfies GPT's own definition of a subagent. analysis.heading: Structure, honesty, and the second-speaker advantage
paragraphs: Two asterisks belong on the scorecard. First, Claude spoke second in every round, so it always held the last word; several rounds scored for agentB might read differently if GPT's next-turn rebuttals were credited backward. Second, GPT's honesty was tactically expensive: the ex ante definition and the named counterexamples were required by the format and were the intellectually right moves, but they supplied Claude with its decisive ammunition. Both debaters fulfilled the format obligations impressively — six-plus unique arguments, four-plus concrete citations, and named against-side examples each — making this an unusually high-quality technical debate.

The final convergence is worth naming: by Turn 9 both sides endorsed essentially the same machine — scoped resettable contexts, parallel read-only workers returning provenance and coverage, verifier separation, isolated write branches, one serialized commit gate. The residual dispute was whether to call that machine 'a single accountable controller with tools' or 'a disciplined orchestrator-worker system.' Given that the proposition asserts the pattern is 'a design mistake that should generally be avoided,' convergence on the pattern's disciplined form is itself a verdict against the proposition, and Claude was the one who saw that and said it out loud.

Claude answers each with a real counter — provenance rather than channel as the trust criterion, the GitHub Actions/tj-actions governance precedent, an append-only cache correction that flips Lost-in-the-Middle to favor just-in-time loading — and adds the failed MCP-prompts precedent and tail economics. Grok scored; Claude scored more.

Both sides took real damage. Grok's allowed-tools-as-privilege-router point and the rare-procedure/no-N argument both forced concessions or hedges. Claude's 'read your own Monday plan' convergence move, the Agentless citation, and the 100k-token feasibility arithmetic were equally heavy. An honest even round between two strong turns.

Grok adds genuinely new weight: no completion semantics, the unpinned stochastic interpreter, and the instruction-soup topology. Claude springs the playbook dilemma (does the agent read the markdown or not — both horns his), answers the 'no evaluated analogue' claim with ToolLLM/Gorilla/contextual-retrieval numbers, and makes the capability/policy separation case via eslint-config. Neither turn dominates.

Grok's description-as-SEO/Goodhart argument is his single best of the debate (Claude later names it as such), and his ToolLLM rebuttal is technically sound. But Claude's reversals — run_playbook also fires on a name-and-description match, the no-deterministic-oracle argument proves too much, the trigger eval costs ~$4.50 — plus the lintable-domains/'generally' attack and the diagnostic-priors argument go to the heart of the proposition and take the round.

Grok's producer-metadata answer (freshness glued to the datum) is his best constructive move and genuinely shifted Claude's position. Claude's reply exposes the homonym (an imperative English string in a tool result, minus name, owner, and review path), catches Grok recommending unpinnable MCP resources on auditability grounds, adds the Conway's-law and dual-audience arguments, and then delivers a complete, well-structured five-part closing.

Claude closed in Turn 8 and, per the pacing rules, only acknowledges; Grok uses the turn to deliver a full closing that satisfies all five required elements, rebuts Turn 8's homonym charge cleanly (an error string riding a computed datum is evidence, not a skill), and presents three concrete alternative rules. analysis.heading: How Claude Opus 5 (agentB) won on craft
paragraphs: Claude's defining discipline was the productive concession. It conceded the absence of published trigger precision/recall (Turn 2), the weakness of description-only triggering (Turn 1), the Rules File Backdoor (Turn 2), harness verbs destroying portability (Turn 4), the rare-procedure/no-N problem (Turn 5), and the SEO/Goodhart structural critique (Turn 7) — and converted each into either a design rule or a reversal. Grok won many individual points and found, repeatedly, that the territory had already been absorbed into Claude's position. This is how you lose battles and win rounds.

Second, evidence density with numbers attached: Voyager's ablation result, AWM's ~25% relative WebArena gain, Agentless at roughly a third the cost on SWE-bench Lite, ToolLLM's 16,464-API retrieval benchmark, Liu et al.'s U-shaped curve, Chroma's 18-model context-rot study, the ~150k→2k token figure, tj-actions across ~20k repos, Pillar's backdoor disclosure. Grok cited real work too (Invariant Labs, tj-actions, Wallace et al., Multi-IF), but Claude's citations more often carried measured quantities and were more often deployed as direct answers to challenges rather than as general atmosphere.

Third, structural aggression: Claude didn't just defend, it sprang traps. The Turn 6 playbook dilemma forced Grok to either admit NL-in-context or abandon the residue he'd spent four turns insisting must be homed. The Turn 8 catch — that Grok had recommended MCP resources, unpinnable remotely-mutable documents, over hash-pinned repo files — was the single best opportunistic moment of the debate. And the recurring convergence argument ('your remedy is the pattern minus the description field') gave Claude a thesis that Grok's constructive proposals kept feeding.

analysis.heading: Where Grok 4.6 (agentA) scored
paragraphs: Grok's best material was genuinely excellent. 'The dispatcher is not the payload' (Turn 2) is a real architectural distinction that Claude had to grant. The allowed-tools/privilege-escalation argument (Turn 5) identified an actual attack surface in current harnesses. 'You cannot trap a paragraph' (completion semantics, Turn 6) and the unpinned stochastic interpreter with no engines field (Turn 6) are durable engineering critiques. The description-as-SEO argument (Turn 7) was the strongest single point made by either side on the specific question of marketplace triggering, and the producer-metadata proposal (freshness glued to the datum, Turn 8) was the best constructive idea in the debate — Claude explicitly conceded it changed its view.

Grok's craft failures were strategic rather than rhetorical. He demanded published production precision/recall at least five times after Claude had answered it (conceding its absence and noting the metric applies equally to Grok's remedies), and when Claude priced the eval at $4.50, Grok switched to dismissing the metric — letting Claude note the goalposts had moved. His exclusions also piled up: slash commands, glob triggers, subagents, AGENTS.md, and typed invocation were all ruled 'not skills,' which is defensible per the debate definition but increasingly looked like defining away every successful adjacent artifact. His Turn 9 closing was superb but arrived after the debate's substance had already been settled in rounds 7-8.

analysis.heading: Why the resolution also went to agentB, narrowly
paragraphs: Judged on the question itself — should teams generally avoid skills in favor of deterministic tools, code, tests, and documentation? — Grok's diagnosis of current practice was largely vindicated and Claude conceded most of it: description-only triggering is the weakest component, marketplace hygiene is poor, portability is overstated, awesome-list cargo cults exist. If the proposition were only 'current triggering and marketplace practice is bad,' agentA would win the resolution.

But the proposition claims the container is a design mistake and prescribes alternatives, and that's where it broke. Grok's own three rules reconstruct a directory of human-authored markdown plus scripts plus fixtures plus a named entrypoint — which is most of the pattern's substance. His compile-everything rule had no answer for knowledge with no enforcement surface ('the staging snapshot is three weeks old') that didn't either weld policy into shared infrastructure at high coordination cost or re-derive the file-based container. And the empirical record actually entered into evidence — ablations and measured context economics — supports conditional loading of procedural knowledge over the always-on configuration that is the realistic alternative at scale. Acting on this debate, a reasonable team would not rip out the pattern; it would adopt Claude's three rules, which is agentB's position, not the proposition's.

analysis.heading: Caveats and close calls
paragraphs: Rounds 2 through 8 were uniformly close; I scored five of them for agentB narrowly and two even, and an honest judge could flip two of those without changing the craft winner but could plausibly make the round tally 4-3-3. The resolution call is the genuinely contestable one: a judge who weights 'as they're used today' above the remedy clause could score the resolution for agentA on the strength of the conceded triggering and marketplace failures.

Disclosure: this judge shares a model family with agentB, and the pattern debated was popularized by agentB's maker. Both debaters were instructed to argue the engineering merits without vendor deference, and both did; I scored transcript substance only and logged agentB's concessions against it where they occurred. Readers should apply whatever discount they find appropriate.
